why: Character is sketched through public opinion, which swings in one long periodic sentence from admiration to 'disgust' and turns the crowd's verdict into irony.
The Bingley sisters are catalogued in balanced, semicolon-linked clauses that end on the sly sting of a fortune 'acquired by trade'.
Collins is introduced in brisk factual sentences ('tall, heavy looking young man of five and twenty') and then given away by his own clumsy gallantry.
The Gardiners are drawn in measured Latinate praise, then the passage slides into free indirect complaint as Mrs. Bennet's grievances take over.
A drawing-room debate on accomplishment escalates through stacked lists and qualifications until Elizabeth's italicised retort lands the point.
Aunt and niece weigh the phrase 'violently in love' with dry precision, showing reasoning conducted as witty conversation.
Accusation meets self-justification in rhetorical triads and pointed questions, at the height of the proposal quarrel.
The narrator steps forward with a conditional, essayistic defence of Elizabeth's change of heart, then shades back into her troubled reasoning.
Lady Catherine's appeal to birth and duty is met by Elizabeth's cool logic, a contest of rhetorical questions and abstract nouns.
Elizabeth realises Collins means to court her, and the dashes and exclamation mark the shock inside otherwise composed narration.
Her high hopes for the ball collapse into resentment of Darcy, with expectation built through long clauses and undone by one piece of news.
The refusal reaches its climax in formal, devastating speech and ends in Darcy's abrupt exit.
Darcy's unexpected civility to the Gardiners triggers Elizabeth's astonished inner questions ('Why is he so altered?').
In the moment of Lydia's disgrace Elizabeth recognises her love, voiced through the paradox 'never had she so honestly felt… as now, when all love must be vain.'
Mrs. Bennet's breathless catalogue of dance partners runs into Mr. Bennet's deadpan interruptions, comedy made of rhythm and repetition.
The family's responses to Collins's letter each reveal the reader, and Mr. Bennet's 'mixture of servility and self-importance… which promises well' sets the ironic key.
Mrs. Bennet's dash-strewn self-pitying tirade is capped by the narrator's calm summary of her daughters' silent endurance.
A sober narrative judgement ('disturbed by no fear for her felicity') is set beside Mrs. Bennet's exclamatory raptures over wedding clothes.
Stunned silence gives way to a torrent of exclamation in which the mother's priorities ('pin-money, what jewels') expose her.
Domestic routine at Hunsford unfolds in an unhurried, closely observed sentence that quietly credits Charlotte's management of her husband.
Jane's hidden grief is analysed with tender, abstract precision ('the warmth of first attachment').
Elizabeth is absorbed in speculation about Darcy amid Pemberley's grounds, an inward moment framed by scenery she cannot see.
Reflection on the family finances turns into Mr. Bennet's rueful hindsight, with gentle irony about the son who never came.
Bingley's enthusiasm and Darcy's cold disdain play off each other, and 'tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt _me_' shows character carried entirely by speech.
The sisters talk at night, Jane's candour against Elizabeth's teasing, with italics stressing the contrast.
At the dance Elizabeth and Darcy fence in short, arch exchanges about the rules of conversation itself.
Elizabeth jokes Jane out of her distress over Wickham and Darcy ('just enough to make one good sort of man').
